result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.complement()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Return the complement of the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L11559-L11652){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.complement() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Complement](/assets/graphs/op-complement.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="On the left, a four-node graph with three edges forming an open path A - B - C - D. On the right, the same nodes with the complementary set of three edges (the ones absent from the original graph) shown in the accent color." width="100%"} Creates a new graph with the same nodes but complementary edges. An edge exists in the complement if and only if it does *not* exist in the original graph. Self-loops are never included. New edges have no attributes and default weight (`1.0` for weighted graphs). For directed graphs, complements directed edges independently in each direction. For undirected graphs, complements undirected edges. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new Graph with complementary edge set. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#80c09f74 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge("A", "B") ) comp = graph.complement() comp.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: Every pair that wasn't connected in the original now is, and vice versa: ::: {#c597e557 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} comp.has_edge("A", "C"), comp.has_edge("A", "B") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: ::: This makes it easy to find missing connections in a network -- for example, spotting which pairs of people in a friend graph aren't yet friends: ::: {#53e7b621 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} friends = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="Alice") .add_node(label="Bob") .add_node(label="Charlie") .add_node(label="Diana") .add_edge("Alice", "Bob") .add_edge("Bob", "Charlie") ) non_friends = friends.complement() non_friends.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['Charlie--Diana', 'Alice--Charlie', 'Alice--Diana', 'Bob--Diana'] ``` ::: ::: Comparing a graph to its own complement is one way to check for self-complementary structure: ::: {#9d7e3a29 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_node(label="A") g.add_node(label="B") g.add_node(label="C") g.add_node(label="D") g.add_edge("A", "B") g.add_edge("C", "D") comp = g.complement() comp.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['A--C', 'A--D', 'B--C', 'B--D'] ``` ::: ::: Directed graphs are complemented per-direction, so a missing `A->B` doesn't imply `B->A` was also missing: ::: {#2fb2b713 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge("A", "B") ) comp = g.complement() comp.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` ['B->C', 'B->A', 'C->B', 'C->A', 'A->C'] ``` ::: :::
